note: Aquitaine — one of the great fiefs of medieval France, held by the English crown as a remnant of the Angevin Empire — was gradually absorbed into France through the Hundred Years' War. English Gascony (the southern portion of Aquitaine) was the prize that sustained English involvement in France; it provided Bordeaux's wine trade revenues, which funded English military operations. The Battle of Castillon (1453) ended the last English attempt to hold Gascony; Bordeaux surrendered in October 1453. The absorption ended 300 years of English continental presence and transferred France's richest wine-producing region to direct royal control.

_quarry.structural_significance: Aquitaine's absorption completes the French monarchy's consolidation of all major fiefs into the royal domain; the Bordelais wine trade, previously funding English military operations, now enriches the French crown; the completion of Capetian-Valois territorial consolidation creates the France that enters the 16th century as Europe's dominant power
